name: Levels of processing
statement: What a person does with material at study, rather than how long or how hard they work at it, determines how much of it they later remember.
meaning: Two claims travel under this name and they are not equally well supported. The first is an experimental result. Judge a word for its meaning and you will recognise it later; judge the same word for its typeface and you will not. The second is the framework Craik and Lockhart built around that result: perception runs through levels from surface features to meaning, the memory trace is a by-product of however far that analysis got, and trace persistence rises with depth. The framework carries three further commitments that the effect itself does not need. Repeating an analysis at one level should buy nothing. Deeper traces should decay more slowly. And depth should be an independent property of the encoding, not a label read backwards off the memory score. Each of the three has been tested. The result holds; the commitments have fared worse, and Craik withdrew several of them within three years.

origin.who: Fergus I. M. Craik and Robert S. Lockhart
origin.where: Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior
origin.note: The paper reports no experiments. It reviews the case for multistore models of memory, argues that their inconsistencies are better handled by looking at encoding operations, and proposes depth as the organising variable. Its own summary of its status is flat: the approach "does not constitute a theory of memory" but offers "a set of orienting attitudes". Craik and Lockhart also conceded on the page that "spread" would describe their idea more accurately than "depth", and kept "depth" because it "conveys the flavor of our argument".

evidence: The demonstration everyone cites is Craik and Tulving's ten experiments of 1975, run at Toronto and framed to subjects as a study of perception. In Experiment 1, 20 paid college students saw 40 words in a tachistoscope, each preceded by one of five questions. Is a word present, is it in capital letters, does it rhyme with a given word, is it in a given category, would it fit a given sentence frame. An unexpected recognition test followed, a sheet of the 40 study words among 40 distractors, of which any one subject had seen 36. Recognition of words answered yes ran .22, .18, .78, .93 and .96 across those five questions, and words answered no ran .14, .36, .63 and .83. Median decision latencies climbed with the question, 591 to 746 ms for yes responses, F(4, 171) = 35.4, p < .001, and the recognition effect of question type was F(3, 133) = 52.8, p < .001. Craik and Tulving put the mismatch plainly: 200 msec of extra study time led to a 400% improvement in retention. Experiment 2 tightened the design with 24 subjects, three question types and 120 distractors. Recognition of yes words rose from 15% after a typescript question to 81% after a sentence question, F(2, 46) = 118, p < .001; no words rose from 19% to 49%. Experiment 5 is the one that decides between depth and time. A shallow task, judging whether a word matched a consonant-vowel pattern such as CCVVC, took 1.70 and 1.74 sec against .83 and .88 sec for the sentence task, and it produced worse recognition, .57 and .50 against .82 and .69, F(1, 23) = 40.9, p < .001. A slow shallow task loses to a fast deep one. The experiments also turned up something the framework did not predict. Words that fitted their question were remembered better than words that did not, .93 against .63 for category questions, although yes and no decisions took the same time. Craik and Tulving read this as elaboration rather than depth, and it is why the 1975 paper takes up Schulman's principle of congruity as a separate factor. The principle is Schulman's, published in 1974; the 1975 paper adopts it rather than coining it.

examples.text: Somebody who reads a report for typos can rarely say afterwards what it argued, while a colleague who read it for the argument can summarise it. The two spent the same minutes on the same pages, and what they did with the words set what stayed.

A student copies out a definition twice and recalls little of it a week on. Another spends the same minutes deciding which of two cases the definition covers, and remembers it. The work was equal; only one of them handled the meaning.

Repeating a new colleague's name silently while shaking hands is a poor way to keep it. Working out whether the name suits the person, or what it rhymes with, gives it something to sit on, and the difference shows an hour later at the coffee machine.

replication.headline: Peng, Logie and Della Sala found deep encoding ahead of shallow on immediate recognition in all three of their experiments, partial eta squared 0.34 to 0.57, with 86 and 114 participants analysed and 72 recruited.
replication.detail: The three experiments were run online in two sessions, with recognition tested immediately and again after a delay. Experiment 1 set semantic judgements against rhyme judgements in 86 participants after exclusions, and immediate recognition gave d prime 2.61 for deep against 2.10 for shallow, F(1, 83) = 49.24, p < .001, partial eta squared 0.37. Experiment 2 used the consonant-vowel task from Craik and Tulving's Experiment 5 and recruited 72, and the shallow task again took longer to perform, 3,774 ms against 2,912 ms, while producing worse memory: d prime 1.83 against 2.58, F(1, 66) = 87.43, p < .001, partial eta squared 0.57. The paper gives the exclusion rule for that experiment but never says how many of the 72 survived it, so 72 is a recruited figure and not an analysed one. Experiment 3 moved the manipulation between participants, 114 after exclusions, and gave 2.11 against 2.83, F(1, 108) = 55.45, p < .001, partial eta squared 0.34. The advantage survived every delay tested, 30 minutes to 24 hours in the first two experiments and 30 minutes to six hours in the third, with delayed-recognition effects of partial eta squared 0.25 to 0.35. No experiment found a levels by delay interaction, and the Bayes factors favoured the null at 6.57, 5.76 and 3.21. The forgetting-slope analysis is where the paper is less tidy than its abstract. Fitting power functions gave no difference between the slopes of deep and shallow items in the first two experiments, chi-squared(1) = 2.25, p = .134 and chi-squared(1) = 1.26, p = .262. In Experiment 3 the same fit gave chi-squared(1) = 13.48, p < .001, which says the slopes do differ. The authors set that result aside, arguing that a power function ties its slope to its intercept, and rest Experiment 3 on the analysis of variance and on the logarithmic fit, chi-squared(1) = 0.10, p = .747. Their conclusion, that rates of forgetting are independent of the encoding operations levels of processing manipulates, therefore holds on two of the three experiments outright and on the third by an argued choice of curve. No multi-site or registered replication of the effect was located on 21 September 2026; the searches covered Crossref, Europe PMC and general web search.

study.cite: Peng, N., Logie, R. H., & Della Sala, S. (2025). Effect of levels-of-processing on rates of forgetting. Memory & Cognition, 53(2), 692-709.

limits: The effect is robust and the framework around it is not, which makes the boundary between them the thing worth knowing. Craik and Lockhart proposed that deeper analysis leaves a longer lasting trace. Peng, Logie and Della Sala tested that directly and read their three experiments as parallel forgetting curves: depth sets how much is learned and does nothing to how fast it goes. That reading is sound for the first two experiments and argued for the third, where one of the two curve fits did separate the slopes. The framework also held that repeating an analysis at the same level, what Craik and Lockhart called Type I processing, "does nothing to enhance memory for the stimulus". Two 1977 papers reported otherwise. Nelson's three experiments found that repetition at the phonemic level does help, whether massed or distributed and whether the measure is uncued recall, cued recall or recognition. Glenberg, Smith and Green isolated Type I rehearsal and found that more of it improved recognition, concluding that it "serves more than a maintenance-only function". The strongest empirical objection is Morris, Bransford and Franks. Semantic study beat rhyme study on an ordinary recognition test, and rhyme study beat semantic study when the test asked which words rhymed with a probe. Depth is therefore not a property of encoding alone but of the fit between encoding and test, which is the transfer-appropriate processing account. Craik reports that averaged over their first two experiments the semantic study with semantic test combination still reached 0.68, against 0.40 for rhyme with rhyme. Those two figures are quoted here from his description of that paper and not from the paper, which could not be opened. Craik and Tulving themselves withdrew much of the 1972 apparatus in the same paper that is cited as its confirmation. They abandoned the fixed series of analysers, abandoned decision time as an index of depth, and wrote that "differential depth of encoding does not seem a promising description, except in very general terms" and that many of the 1972 ideas "stand in need of considerable modification". Craik later conceded a further boundary: amnesic patients understand what they are told and still do not remember it, so "deep processing is necessary but not sufficient for later episodic memory".
misreadings: The circularity objection is the one most often garbled. It is normally credited to Baddeley's 1978 paper in Psychological Review, and it does not say the effect is false. It says that without a measure of depth taken independently of memory, the framework cannot be wrong: whatever is well remembered can be relabelled as deeply processed. Craik states it in that form himself and accepts it, writing that the absence of an objective index of depth is a major criticism and that psychology is "stuck for the moment with such unsatisfactory methods as agreement among judges". His own attempted index, decision time, fails in both directions. It fails within the 1975 data, where yes and no decisions took equal time and produced unequal memory, and it fails across materials, because an expert encodes material in their field quickly and remembers it well. Baddeley's paper could not be opened, and the statement of the objection quoted here is Craik's restatement of it, not Baddeley's wording. A second error treats levels of processing as a theory that was tested and beaten. Craik and Lockhart said in the paper that it was not a theory, and its main empirical prediction keeps coming out right. A third error reads depth as effort or as time on task. Craik and Tulving's list of what does not determine retention is explicit: not intention to learn, not the amount of effort, not the difficulty of the task, not the time spent judging, not even the amount of rehearsal. Their Experiment 5 is built to make the point, and Peng and colleagues rebuilt it with the same result. A fourth error is that the effect needs incidental learning, on the reasoning that a subject who knows about the test will process everything deeply. Craik and Tulving got the same pattern under intentional learning in Experiments 4 and 9, and every participant in the 2025 replication was told about the memory test in advance. The last error is quoting the .96 from the 1975 paper as the depth effect. That figure is a sentence question answered yes, and congruity between question and word is a separate factor doing part of the work; the matching no cell is .83, and at the category level the gap is .93 against .63.

sources.text: Craik, F. I. M., & Lockhart, R. S. (1972). Levels of processing: A framework for memory research. Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior, 11(6), 671-684. Read in full from the open copy on the Wixted laboratory's page at the University of California, San Diego, which serves the PDF to a plain request. Every quotation on this page was checked against it.

Craik, F. I. M., & Tulving, E. (1975). Depth of processing and the retention of words in episodic memory. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 104(3), 268-294. Read in full from the open copy on the Rotman Research Institute's publication pages. Every figure on this page comes from its Tables 2 and 4 and its results sections.

Peng, N., Logie, R. H., & Della Sala, S. (2025). Effect of levels-of-processing on rates of forgetting. Memory & Cognition, 53(2), 692-709. Read in full, open access, from Europe PMC's full-text XML route. The forgetting-slope result for Experiment 3 is in its results section and not in its abstract.

Craik, F. I. M. (2002). Levels of processing: Past, present... and future? Memory, 10(5-6), 305-318. The source for Craik's own account of the missing index of depth, of the Morris and colleagues figures, and of the necessary-but-not-sufficient concession. Read in full from the open copy on the Rotman Research Institute's publication pages. Craik is there quoting his own 1999 chapter for the necessary-but-not-sufficient wording.

Baddeley, A. D. (1978). The trouble with levels: A reexamination of Craik and Lockhart's framework for memory research. Psychological Review, 85(3), 139-152. Not read. The obstacle is not a paywall notice: APA PsycNet answers a request for the full text with an Imperva bot block, and ERIC holds only an abstract, which carries no numbers. Tried on 21 September 2026 at PsycNet, ERIC, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and general web search. The circularity objection is quoted on this page from Craik's 2002 restatement of it.

Tried on 21 September 2026 at ScienceDirect, ERIC, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and general web search. The finding is taken from the abstract reproduced by ERIC and the recognition figures from Craik's 2002 description.
